newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Yorks Water improves profits, service.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Yorks Water improves profits, service.

text.p: British water and sewerage firm Yorkshire Water Plc, fiercely criticised two years ago for its handling of a severe drought, turned in higher year profits on Friday and said it aimed to improve performance.
"Customers are our priority and we are investing heavily to secure clean water supply and to improve other areas of service," the company said in a statement.

Yorkshire reported pre-tax profits of 215.8 million pounds ($353.4 million) for the year ending March 31, within expectations and up from 162.2 million pounds last year after exceptional drought costs of 47 million.
It paid out a total dividend of 18.5 pence per share, compared with an adjusted 15.5 pence last year, which takes account of a capital restructuring.
Shares were up just a penny at 376 pence by 0915 GMT.
Chairman Brandon Gough said that the progress in improving supplies which the company had achieved was, "pretty crucial, not just to customer confidence but also investor confidence."

Gough and his team replaced the executives who were strongly criticised two years ago when Yorkshire, operating in one of Britain's wettest areas, was forced to tanker in supplies to cope with a severe drought.
The company narrowly missed having to cut essential domestic supplies in some parts, which would have forced customers to queue for water at public collection points.
Industry regulator Ofwat penalised Yorkshire with a freeze on real price increases for two years and Gough and his team moved in to replace the old management.
Yorkshire has taken steps to improve its ability to handle drought -- Britain is suffering its driest two year period for 200 years -- and now maintains there should be no restrictions this summer.
Even if the conditions of 1995 were repeated, "water restrictions should not prove to be necessary this summer" the company said.
Leakage has fallen to around 26 percent of supplies and the company aims to cut that by another one percent or so this year.
"That'll take us to our 1998 target that we already have," chief executive Kevin Bond said.
The new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has said it will set mandatory leakage targets for companies as part of a 10-point plan aimed at handling the drought.
Finance director Brian Wilson said the company was positive about the plan, adding that it welcomed "the government's commitment, involvement with the industry."
Labour has been severely critical of Britain's water companies and other privatised utilities for turning in hefty profits and shareholder benefits along with fat executive pay packets.

It has vowed to introduce a one-off tax on the "excess profits" of privatised utilities to fund a three billion pound plan to cut unemployment, but details await its first budget expected in June or July.
Wilson said the company had "made an assumption for a windfall tax" in its commitment to growth of 6-8 percent in cash spent on dividends, but declined to name a figure.
Gough said the company took it for granted there was going to be a windfall tax.
"The issue is on what basis will it be levied as much as how much it will be."

"If the government means what it says, that it will be focused on clearly defined excess profits, then we would not view it as penalising us because we don't think that our profits are excess," Gough added. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
